sentences.text: This needle has pointed north your whole life.
But the seafloor remembers further back.
North and south have swapped.
Again and again, with no schedule.
That needle follows a {b}field{/} that wraps the whole planet.
It feels permanent.
It is not.
At ocean ridges, fresh lava cools into rock.
Tiny magnetic grains lock in the {b}field's{/} direction.
The seafloor spreads, and each flip starts a new stripe.
Five million years, about twenty flips, and wildly uneven gaps.
So, two questions.
When will it flip next?
And {metric}how often{/} does it flip?
Which one can we answer?
In a simple computer model of a flipping {b}field{/}, the first is hopeless.
The second is not.
Finding out why takes us through liquid metal and chaos.
Then to {model}machines{/} that dream up snapshots of {b}magnetic fields{/}.
They must obey some laws exactly, and others only on average.
How often does the {b}field{/} flip?
A learner's map of the MilaDy project, from a compass to today's research.
Should the first simulations target {metric}how often{/} the field flips, or the warning signs just before a flip?
Is there a giant magnet hidden inside the Earth?
Deep down, the outer core is an ocean of liquid iron.
Left alone, a {b}field{/} there would fade away within tens of thousands of years.
Yet Earth's field is several billion years old.
So the moving iron must keep making it, all the time.
Take a bar magnet: north at one end, south at the other.
Cut it in half.
You get two magnets, each with a north and a south.
No one has ever found a lone magnetic pole.
{b}Field lines{/} say the same: they never start or stop.
Draw any box, and count.
As many lines go in as come out.
Keep this box in mind.
A bicycle dynamo turns motion into electricity, using a built-in magnet.
The Earth has to make its own. The trick: a loop.
Hold a microphone near its own speaker, and turn up the {param}gain{/}.
Below a certain point, a whisper fades.
Past it, the loop feeds itself.
Now spin a copper disc wired to a coil around its axle.
Current makes {b}field{/}, and field makes current.
Spin it faster and faster. Does the field grow bit by bit, or not at all until some speed?
Not at all, until a threshold.
Past it, each turn multiplies a tiny {b}seed field{/} by the same factor: exponential growth.
Just past the threshold, growth is slow.
Then the field brakes the disc, and growth stops.
Who pays for all this?
A motor drives the {u}flow{/}; in the Earth, convection does.
The flow stretches the field; the field brakes the flow.
Once growth stops, every watt that goes in leaves as heat, on average.
A dynamo turns motion into field; it creates no energy.
Earth's {b}field{/} points one way today. Which way should it prefer?
Reverse every field line: the dynamo's equations read the same.
So, neither. The two directions are mirror twins, equally lawful.
Which one you get is history, not law: in the disc, the seed's sign decides.
And nothing in the laws forbids a flip.
Moving iron, a loop with a threshold, no favourite direction.
But the disc had wires; liquid iron has none.
Then what motion can do it, and how fast?
Near the threshold, should dynamo simulations start from a tiny seed, a strong one, or both?
What kind of motion can grow a {b}magnetic field{/}?
In a perfect conductor, field lines would be threads frozen into the fluid.
Wherever the {u}flow{/} stretches a thread, the field along it grows stronger.
Real metals let the threads smudge, like spreading ink.
The smudging speed is set by the metal's {param}magnetic diffusivity{/}.
Same flow, two metals.
A good conductor smudges slowly: the threads stay sharp.
A poor one smudges fast: the threads blur away.
One number keeps the score: the {param}magnetic Reynolds number{/}, Rm.
It is the {u}flow's speed{/}, times its size, divided by the {param}magnetic diffusivity{/}.
Large Rm: stretching outpaces smudging.
Small Rm: smudging wins.
Turn the Rm knob up, and watch a weak seed field.
At low Rm, the seed dies away.
Past a threshold, the growth rate crosses zero and the seed grows, like the squeal.
Laboratory dynamos use liquid sodium.
It flows as easily as water.
But a field smudges in it about a hundred thousand times faster than its swirls do.
Their ratio, one in a hundred thousand, is the {param}magnetic Prandtl number{/}, Pm.
Reaching an Rm of a few tens takes violent stirring.
The flow's {param}Reynolds number{/}, the gauge of turbulence, reaches millions.
So every laboratory dynamo is turbulent.
Only three liquid-sodium experiments have made their own field, each a different kind.
In Riga, a corkscrew flow made a field that oscillates and slowly turns.
In Karlsruhe, fifty-two spiralling cells made a steady field, close to a {b}dipole{/}.
And only VKS, at Cadarache, made a dipole that can flip.
A fourth, DRESDYN in Dresden, aims to join them: a spinning cylinder whose axis slowly turns.
Inside VKS: a cylinder holding a hundred and fifty litres of liquid sodium.
At its ends, two bladed discs, the impellers, spin in opposite directions.
Should it matter what metal the discs are made of?
With stainless steel discs, there was no dynamo, even at full speed.
Swap in discs of soft iron, and a dipole grows along the axis.
So the threshold depends on more than Rm: materials count too.
Now spin the two discs at different speeds.
At some settings, the dipole flips again and again, with no schedule.
Like the compass needle at the start, but every minute or two.
Each flip itself takes only about five seconds.
Uneven stripes, like the seafloor's, but written in minutes, not millions of years.
Simulations cannot reach sodium's tiny {param}Pm{/}: which Pm values should the first three-dimensional runs cover?
Riga, Karlsruhe and VKS crowned a hunt of nearly a century.
Here is its map.
Lane one, the Earth's record: lavas magnetized backwards, nineteen oh six.
Seafloor stripes, nineteen sixty-three.
Then flips as chance events, whose odds change over the ages.
Lane two, theory.
Nineteen nineteen: a moving, conducting fluid might keep the Sun's field alive.
Nineteen thirty-three: no flow can sustain a field that is symmetric around an axis.
Nineteen fifty-eight: the first proven examples of flows that can.
In the seventies came simple dynamo flows, later the blueprints of Riga and Karlsruhe.
Lane three: building a dynamo.
Nineteen sixty-three: a model dynamo of spinning iron cylinders.
Nineteen ninety-nine: sodium makes its own field, in Riga, then Karlsruhe.
Two thousand six: VKS, only with iron discs, then the first flips of a turbulent sodium dynamo.
Lane four, computers.
Nineteen eighty-one: simulated turbulence grows dynamos.
Nineteen ninety-five: a simulated Earth's core reverses its field.
Ringed pins mark papers co-signed by this project's supervisors.
Nineteen ninety-seven: two simulated counter-rotating eddies make a dynamo.
Two thousand five: such dynamos still work at a {param}Pm{/} of one hundredth.
From twenty sixteen, two codes simulate the VKS tank, iron impellers included.
Twenty twenty-six: both make it flip, in the runs explored only with conducting surroundings.
Their reference run: a {param}Reynolds number{/} near sixteen hundred, not millions.
Lane five: a few dials instead of a tank.
Nineteen fifty-eight: two coupled disc dynamos already flip.
Twenty twelve: three dials that flip by chaos alone; we will play with them soon.
Twenty twenty-six: four dials fitted to the simulated VKS flips, by a method that finds equations in data.
MilaDy began in twenty twenty-six, bringing machine learning where tanks, computers and dials meet.
Yet the data-driven lane is thin: in twenty twenty-two, the learning methods one study tried could not reliably foresee a geomagnetic flip.
The internship and a proposed thesis add a bet: {model}machines{/} that dream up dynamo fields and obey their physics.
Behind every lane, the same race: stretching against smudging.
Back to the race: the {u}flow{/} stretches the field, and diffusion smudges it.
Physicists write the very same race as a single equation.
On the left: how fast the {b}magnetic field{/} changes, at each point.
First term on the right: the flow carries the field along and stretches it, like the threads.
Second term: diffusion smudges it, at a pace set by the magnetic diffusivity.
A poor conductor smudges fast.
Stretching against smudging: the whole race, in one line.
Picture the {u}flow{/} as a conveyor belt that does not feel its cargo.
A weak {b}field{/} rides on the imposed flow, and fades or grows exponentially.
On a log scale: a straight line, whose slope is the growth rate.
But a strong field pushes back on the flow, as it braked the copper disc: the line bends into a plateau.
These are the kinematic and dynamic regimes.
Flips live on the plateau.
To test ideas, physicists need a {u}flow{/} simple enough to write on one line, yet able to make a dynamo.
One classic choice: the ABC flow.
It fills space with identical twisting rooms.
Three crossed winds make the fluid corkscrew: it spins around the direction it moves.
This box returns higher on our climb.
Now turn one {param}knob{/} on this flow: Rm. Turning it up means less diffusion.
Less smudging should only help the stretching.
So once the dynamo switches on, it stays on. Right?
Here is the growth rate, computed at twenty-four settings.
Below about nine, every {b}field{/} fades. Then growth turns positive: the dynamo is on.
Near seventeen and a half, it switches off again.
Above about twenty-seven, it comes back.
Not one threshold, but windows: turning a knob further does not always help.
It agrees with published results. No machine learning yet: this only tests the solver.
Real dynamos have not one {param}knob{/}, but a panel.
How hard the metal is stirred; how well it conducts.
What the discs are made of: remember the iron.
How unequal their speeds are: that is when VKS flipped.
For DRESDYN, a precessing tank: how fast its axis turns.
Even the wall counts: in VKS simulations, changing only its magnetic condition raised the threshold by about forty percent.
Every turbulent dynamo simulation in three dimensions is very costly.
So only a handful of knob settings get simulated.
Each one is a mountain of data: a single snapshot can weigh more than a gigabyte.
Each run holds only a few flips.
And between the dots, there is nothing at all.
Those gaps are where this film lives.
The study behind this film asks three things.
One: can a {model}machine{/} learn the whole family of fields, even at knob settings between the dots?
Two: can it respect each law where it holds, exactly in every field, or {metric}on average{/} over many fields?
Three: can it tell us {metric}how often{/} the field flips?
To find out, the study's plan climbs a staircase, from three numbers to the shapes of real experiments.
One honest note: this independent study is prospective, built on small experiments on an ordinary computer, and not endorsed by MilaDy, its partners or the supervisors.
An equation, windows, a panel of knobs, a handful of dots.
Full simulations cost too much, so we start with a three-dial caricature that already flips.
Can anyone say when it flips next?
With only a handful of runs, should the {param}settings{/} be spread evenly, or packed near each threshold?
Here is the caricature: three dials, linked by springs.
One is the {b}dipole{/}, the north-south part of the field.
One is the {b}quadrupole{/}, a four-pole part.
The third is a {u}flow{/} pattern, driven by a knob, {param}Gamma{/}.
Three short equations, from Gissinger, tie them together.
Flip both field dials, and the equations read the same.
Three dials, three numbers: the bottom step of the staircase.
Use two dials as a map: {b}quadrupole{/} across, {b}dipole{/} up.
With the knob low, the state circles in one whirlpool, and stays.
A mirror twin circles the mirror whirlpool: dipole down.
Each start is trapped. The dipole never changes sign.
Now turn {param}Gamma{/} up.
Just above zero point eight six, the whirlpools touch: a narrow corridor opens.
The state lingers on one side, then slips through. The {b}dipole{/} flips.
Nothing here is random. So, will the flips come like clockwork?
No. Long waits and short ones, irregularly.
The dipole's sign prints uneven stripes, like the seafloor.
Now count: one tick each time the {b}dipole{/} crosses zero.
Not every tick is a flip: an excursion can cross and come straight back.
Ticks per unit of time: the {metric}crossing rate{/}.
Up to zero point eight six: silence.
Just above, about two ticks per thousand time units.
At {param}Gamma{/} equal to one, about eleven.
Set {param}Gamma{/} at zero point nine, and launch two copies, one millionth apart.
We know the state to six decimals. Can we predict the date of the next flip?
At first, the copies move as one.
But their gap nearly triples every eleven time units.
After about a hundred and fifty, they disagree completely.
The average wait between crossings is longer: over two hundred.
Each extra decimal buys only about twenty-five more time units.
So the forecast fades before the average wait ends. Only the statistics survive.
The path is lost, so leave the shutter open.
Each pass leaves a little light: a glow builds.
A copy started on the other side first paints the mirror image.
Given time, both paint the same glow.
Where does the {b}dipole{/} spend its time? Two humps, the same for both.
This reproducible glow is the stationary distribution.
Below the threshold, each start paints its own whirlpool.
Now film the trajectory, one frame every two time units.
Neighbouring frames look alike.
Cut the film into frames.
Drop them in a shoebox, shake, and throw away the timestamps.
Pour the box out: the frames redraw the same glow.
Each frame is a snapshot: three dial readings, nothing more.
It carries no timestamp and no time order.
Yet the shoebox, plus the equations, answers many questions.
Averages, energy budgets, even how often the dipole crosses zero.
Pick one photo. Its three dial readings give its energy.
From that photo alone, the equations tell how fast its energy changes.
Drop one marble per photo at that value.
Some photos are gaining energy, others losing it. The pile spreads wide.
Yet its average sits at zero.
Energy in equals energy out, on average.
Like a bank account: over the years, income matches spending, yet each day gains or loses.
This is a {metric}law of the crowd{/}. It holds for the shoebox, not for each photo.
How many independent snapshots does each setting need, and how far apart must they be saved?
A puzzle. How many cars cross this line each hour?
No clock. Just one photo from above, where every speedometer can be read.
Can one photo, with no time in it, give you a rate?
It can. Draw a thin strip around the line.
A fast car spends little time inside, so catching one there counts for more.
Add up the speeds of the cars inside, and divide by the strip's width.
On average, that is how many cars cross per hour.
Back to the shoebox. Spread its photos out by their {b}dipole{/} reading.
The line to cross is zero: draw a thin strip around it.
Each photo also needs a speedometer.
No clock required: the dipole's equation turns the photo's three dial readings into a speed.
Up or down, both count, so keep only its size.
Add the speeds inside the strip, then divide by its width and by the total number of photos.
Out comes the {metric}crossing rate{/}.
Shrink the strip to nothing, and for well-behaved systems the recipe is exact: Rice's formula.
The catch: few photos land in a thin strip. Here, about two dozen out of eight thousand.
Now test it against the truth.
At forty-one settings of {param}Gamma{/}, long simulations count the crossings as they happen.
Rice gets only the true snapshots, shuffled, plus the equations.
The two curves almost coincide.
Shade the gap, and divide by the area under the counted curve: the {metric}cumulative error{/}.
Four percent near the threshold, six percent above it.
A good sign, on three chaotic dials that are not even guaranteed to be well-behaved.
One caution: Rice counts crossings, not reversals.
An excursion across zero and back adds two crossings, but no reversal.
To isolate reversals, the PhD plan counts crossings of a far level, on the other side.
So Rice needs only snapshots and the equations, but plenty of snapshots, and cheap ones.
Yet real dynamo simulations exist at only a few {param}knob settings{/}.
Between the dots, there is no shoebox at all.
How do you get snapshots at a setting nobody simulated?
For VKS, which dipole should Rice count, and what threshold turns a crossing into a reversal?
New snapshots start as pure noise: a round cloud of random points.
Over it, the crowd we want: one point per snapshot. Here, two mirror blobs, like the two whirlpools.
Now let a {model}wind{/} blow through the cloud.
Each point drifts, bends, and lands inside the shape of the data.
Fresh noise in, fresh snapshots out, as many as you like.
That wind is a {model}generative model{/}: new, plausible examples, on demand.
The whole game is learning the wind.
One warning before the formulas.
The wind runs on its own {model}transport clock{/}, from zero to one.
Not physical time: at the end, you hold one snapshot, not a movie.
And the {model}wind's arrows{/} move snapshots, not fluid: they are not the {u}fluid's velocity{/}.
How is the wind learned? With a simple trick.
Keep one coordinate of each point, and lay the transport clock out to the right.
Pair each noise point with a random snapshot; join them with a straight string.
Thousands of strings, crossing everywhere.
Pick one place, at one moment.
Several strings pass through, pointing different ways.
The network learns one arrow there: their {model}average direction{/}.
That is the whole training: plain regression, like fitting a curve through points.
Follow the averaged wind, not the strings.
The paths bend, and drawn against the clock, they never cross.
Learn the average exactly, and the noise lands exactly on the data's crowd.
Now give the wind a {param}knob{/}.
Turn it: the target changes shape, and the {model}cloud{/} follows.
One network, every setting.
On the three dials, a real network trained at the filled dots.
It was tested at the open dots, never seen in training.
In between, no theorem promises success: only tests can tell.
Beyond the range, nothing was tested.
At an open dot, the network's {model}snapshots{/} join the shoebox, beside simulated ones.
A generated snapshot has no true twin, so we compare crowds.
Picture each crowd as a pile of sand.
A {metric}distribution distance{/} scores how different the two piles are.
The earth-mover kind counts how much sand must move, and how far.
A perfect model, scored against the data: will it get zero?
No. Roll a fair die a thousand times, then a thousand more.
Same die, same truth, yet the two histograms differ.
That gap is the {metric}noise floor{/}, about what a perfect model scores.
Judge every model against it, at equal sample size, never against zero.
One catch: the samples must be independent.
Overlap them, and the floor drops too low, as the report warns.
Which statistics must the generated fields match, and how close to the noise floor counts as success?
Physics hands the machine two kinds of laws.
Some hold for every single snapshot.
Others hold only for the crowd.
Two shelves, still empty.
Back to the three dials, at a {param}Gamma{/} never seen in training.
Grey: true snapshots.
Violet: a plain {model}generator{/}.
The shape is right.
Now weigh the sides.
The truth is balanced; the machine is not.
Only about four in ten of its snapshots point up.
It copied its data: below the threshold, each run stays in one whirlpool, and the runs split unevenly.
Two ways to teach the mirror.
The first student, data augmentation, sees each training snapshot flipped half the time.
The second, equivariance, has the mirror built into its wind: a mirrored noise point always lands on the mirrored snapshot.
At a {param}Gamma{/} neither has seen, who stays balanced?
The built-in mirror.
The first student tilts a little.
Yet in the mirror's crowd, each snapshot still points one way.
The mirror balances the crowd, not each snapshot.
Its card goes on the crowd shelf: built in, exactly.
Here is that tilt, setting by setting.
Below the threshold, runs often split unevenly: at zero point eight six, only five of sixteen runs point up.
The plain {model}machine{/} copies the imbalance, and spills it onto unseen settings.
Augmentation sits on the {metric}noise floor{/} at its training settings.
Between them, it drifts: the network fills the gaps freely.
The built-in mirror stays on the floor everywhere.
Flipped copies teach the mirror only where there are data.
Can the energy budget catch the tilt?
No. Each whirlpool balances its own budget.
So a mix of the two passes, in any proportion.
On a check of crowd laws, the most lopsided machine even edges ahead.
The mirror needs its own tool.
Remember the budget of the shoebox.
Snapshot by snapshot, energy rises or falls.
Only the crowd balances, on average, like a bank account over the years.
Now, a tempting fix for the machine.
Force every generated snapshot to balance its budget exactly. Better, or worse?
Worse.
Push each snapshot until its energy stops changing: the wide pile collapses into a spike at zero.
A ledger where every single day balances.
No real account looks like that.
The {metric}distribution distance{/} to the truth grows ninefold.
A short proof says why: even a perfect generator, forced this way, cannot match the truth.
So the budget goes on the crowd shelf.
On the next test bench, a cruder score is fooled by such a spike.
Impose the budget on the crowd, during training.
Draw a batch of snapshots at any {param}Gamma{/}, even without data.
Average their energy change and square it: this penalty, the crowd loss, vanishes only when the crowd balances.
But there is a trap.
Even for a balanced crowd, a batch's average wobbles; its square grows with the scatter.
So training also squeezes the scatter, nudging every snapshot toward balance: toward the spike.
It showed up while building this experiment.
The fix: split the batch into two independent juries and multiply their averages.
On average, the scatter drops out, leaving only the crowd's imbalance.
Does it pay off? The next tests will tell.
In three dimensions, which budgets should generated fields meet on average, and must their spread match too?
New test bench: whole fields, not three dials.
A flat square of conducting fluid, its edges wrapping around.
In blue, the swirl of the {u}flow{/}; in vermillion, the electric currents behind the {b}field{/}.
One knob, {param}eta{/}: how fast the field smudges.
But a flat world cannot sustain a dynamo.
Here a random forcing keeps the field alive: a training ground for laws, not a dynamo.
Every training field passes the box test: it is divergence-free.
Train a plain {model}generator{/} on them.
Will its fields be divergence-free?
No.
Now lines appear and vanish inside the box.
Relative to the field's own variations, the divergence is zero point four one: a defect of order one.
A soft penalty only lowers it to zero point three four for the {u}flow{/}, zero point one six for the {b}field{/}.
And the magnetic energy comes out two point seven times too high.
This law belongs on the shelf for every snapshot.
First fix: draw a hill map, not arrows, and let the {u}flow{/} run along its contour lines.
Where the lines crowd, it runs faster, so nothing piles up or leaks, whatever the landscape.
The box agrees: lines in, lines out.
So the {model}machine{/} draws two hill maps, for the {u}flow{/} and the {b}field{/}: zero divergence by construction, however badly it is trained.
Second fix, for any field: split it into swirl plus slope, and delete the slope.
Wave by wave, remove the part of each arrow along the wave's own direction.
The gauges fall to rounding error, down to ten to the minus seventeen.
Measured, though, with the very operator used to enforce it.
Back to the plain {model}generator{/}: why does it miss, trained on clean data?
Follow the part of a field breaking the law.
To bring it exactly to zero, the {model}wind{/} must act as a spring that turns infinitely stiff as the transport clock runs out.
A bounded network cannot, and a sampler with finite steps cannot follow either.
A gap of order one remains: almost is not exactly.
Now the crowd law: on average, energy in equals energy out.
Three ways to impose it, at settings of {param}eta{/} never seen.
One: during training, the crowd loss, with its two juries.
Against a control run of equal length, the {metric}distribution distance{/} drops from two point five to zero point seven.
The control itself gains nothing.
Two: after training, reweight the generated crowd.
Where the model is worst, a poll of five hundred shrinks to one person, and the crowd gets worse.
Three: rescale every snapshot onto the budget.
Each snapshot now dissipates the same: a spike, under a thousandth of the true spread.
Yet the same {metric}distribution distance{/}, built on spectra, improves: it is fooled.
Only the spread gives the spike away. The crowd loss shows no spike.
One training seed each, interpolation only, every model far above the noise floor.
Back to the two shelves, now full.
For every snapshot: zero divergence. Build it in, or project, and it holds exactly; a penalty only roughly.
For the crowd: the energy budget. Impose it on the crowd during training. Reweighting afterwards fails where the model is poor; forcing it onto each snapshot makes a spike.
And the mirror? Each snapshot is lopsided, so it is a crowd law, yet a network can carry it exactly, built in.
One rule sorts them all: enforce each law where it is true.
Put the pieces together: the machine this study proposes.
A {model}wind{/} carries noise to a symmetric crowd of codes, mirror built in.
A decoder turns each code into hill maps, so every field is divergence-free.
And the energy budget is imposed on the crowd.
It has not been built as a whole: the experiments tested pieces, on three dials and a flat sheet, with small networks on an ordinary processor.
One question remains: from snapshots, how well can we answer {metric}how often{/}?
In the partners' solver snapshots, which laws hold exactly, and under which discrete operator?
An aside: the five statements behind the pictures.
Each is elementary; what matters is its exact scope.
The first is almost too simple.
Suppose every field a {model}decoder{/} can draw obeys a linear law, like zero divergence.
Then every sample obeys it, whatever the {model}crowd of codes{/}, however badly trained.
The proof is one line.
The work is in the decoder: hill maps in two dimensions, a vector potential in three, with its gauge fixed.
Second: the spring, in full.
If the data lie in a flat subspace, the ideal {model}wind{/} splits in two.
Along it, a part a network can learn.
Across it, a pull back: the stray part, divided by the time left on the clock.
Followed exactly, that pull lands every sample in the subspace.
Trained perfectly, the plain generator, both projections and hill maps give the same crowd.
Cap the pull, and an order-one stray part survives.
Now add a small, bounded error to the exact pull. Does a stray part survive?
No. The pull erases it.
So the plain generator's zero point four one reads as a missing pull, not a small error.
And the projected flow's tiny residue? Single precision.
Third: penalties. A common one tests the {model}model's guess{/} of where its path will end.
With the ideal wind, that guess averages the data that could lie ahead.
For a linear law, an average of lawful fields is lawful: the penalty vanishes at the optimum, and moves nothing.
Off the optimum, in a real network, it holds the law only roughly.
For a curved law, that fails: two points on a circle average to a point inside.
This is the Jensen gap: now the penalty biases the optimum itself.
Fourth: the mirror, as a theorem.
Make the {model}wind{/} equivariant: mirror a point, and its arrow mirrors too.
Start from noise that looks the same in the mirror.
Then every path has a mirror twin.
So the generated crowd is exactly symmetric at every {param}knob setting{/}, even with lopsided or missing data.
If every true crowd is symmetric, averaging a wind with its mirror never raises the expected loss.
The cost: two network passes instead of one.
In the VKS cylinder, a half-turn swapping the two impellers is a second symmetry.
If their speeds differ, it also flips the sign of that difference, the {param}forcing asymmetry{/}.
The same proof covers it, untested so far.
Last, crowd laws. The equations give any quantity a rate of change at each snapshot.
If the crowd is stationary, that rate {metric}averages to zero{/}, for every quantity; the energy budget is one case.
The proof: let every snapshot run for a moment.
The crowd looks the same, so no average moves: the mean rate is zero.
Necessary, not sufficient: a crowd parked on an unstable fixed point passes every such test.
So does an unstable loop.
The fit to data must therefore stay in the loss.
Can we simulate only one sign of forcing asymmetry, and let the impeller swap supply the other?
Earlier, a {metric}distribution distance{/} meant moving sand.
The experiments mainly use a cousin, built from pairs.
Each dot is a snapshot.
Average every distance across the two crowds, and double it.
Subtract the average distance within each crowd.
Zero means the same law.
Reweighting, up close.
The {model}model's{/} crowd misses its target average.
Leave every snapshot in place; change only how much each counts.
Many weightings hit the target.
The least distorting one is an exponential tilt, known as the I-projection.
Picture crowds as points: those with the right average lie on a line.
The tilted crowd is the foot of the perpendicular.
Any other fix pays the tilt's cost plus an extra, as in Pythagoras.
And nothing moves: the tilted crowd lives only where the model's crowd was.
How much is left of a reweighted crowd?
